assessment.summary: A present, quantified global decline in species and ecosystems — up to a million species threatened with extinction and most of the land and ocean already altered — with cascading risk to the food, water, and climate systems it underpins. IPBES's 2024 assessment found reform-oriented conservation has largely failed to reverse the decline, and its February 2026 business assessment finds finance flows harmful to nature outweighing conservation and restoration spending by more than thirty to one, with under 1% of publicly reporting companies disclosing their biodiversity impacts.
assessment.timeframe: Ongoing decline over recent decades, with many losses (species extinctions, ecosystem tipping points) becoming irreversible within decades absent action.

claims.text: Up to 1 million species are threatened with extinction, many within decades, more than ever before in human history (IPBES Global Assessment, 2019).
75 percent of the terrestrial environment has been severely altered to date by human actions, and 66 percent of the marine environment (IPBES Global Assessment, 2019).
The current rate of global species extinction is tens to hundreds of times higher than the average over the last 10 million years, and it is accelerating (IPBES Global Assessment, 2019).

The cost of delaying actions to halt and reverse biodiversity loss and nature's decline around the world by even a decade is estimated to be double that of acting now (IPBES Transformative Change Assessment, approved 18 December 2024 in Windhoek, Namibia).

In 2023, global public and private finance flows with directly negative impacts on nature were estimated at $7.3 trillion, of which private finance accounted for $4.9 trillion, with public spending on environmentally harmful subsidies of about $2.4 trillion (IPBES Business and Biodiversity Assessment, approved at the 12th session of the IPBES Plenary in Manchester, United Kingdom, February 2026).

$220 billion in public and private finance flows were directed in 2023 to activities contributing to the conservation and restoration of biodiversity, representing just 3% of the public funds and incentives that encourage harmful business behaviour or prevent behaviour beneficial to biodiversity (IPBES Business and Biodiversity Assessment, February 2026).

Less than 1% of publicly reporting companies mention their impacts on biodiversity in their reports; the assessment was prepared by 79 leading experts from 35 countries and approved by representatives of the more than 150 member Governments of IPBES (IPBES Business and Biodiversity Assessment, February 2026).

description: An accelerating, human-driven decline in species and ecosystems that underpin food, water, and climate stability. Nature is being altered at a global scale and pace unprecedented in human history, with a growing share of the ecosystem services humanity depends on already in decline. IPBES's 2024 Transformative Change Assessment found that reform-oriented conservation has largely failed to halt or reverse this decline, and that delaying corrective action by even a decade roughly doubles its eventual cost. Its Business and Biodiversity Assessment, approved in February 2026, traces how the money still runs the other way: in 2023 roughly $7.3 trillion of public and private finance flows had directly negative impacts on nature, against $220 billion directed to conservation and restoration, while under 1% of publicly reporting companies disclose their biodiversity impacts at all.
name: Biodiversity Loss and Ecosystem Collapse
